1      Pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure (“FRCP”) 26, Plaintiff Green Jeeva LLC 
2  (“Plaintiff”)  and  Defendants  Lokesh  Pathak  and  McLob  America  LLC  (together, 
3  “Defendants”), through their respective counsel, hereby stipulate, subject to the Court’s 
4  approval, to stay discovery pending resolution of Defendants’ Motions to Dismiss Plaintiff’s 
5  Complaint filed on October 15, 2025 pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b), 
6  subsections (2), (3), and (6) (“Motions”) (ECF Nos. 26 and 27).        
7      Both Motions argue that this Court does not have personal jurisdiction over either 
8  Defendant nor is venue appropriate or convenient in this District when there is ongoing 
9  proceedings in India that Defendants claim address the same subject matter as Plaintiff’s 
10  claims in this action.  Based upon estimates of the Indian criminal proceedings, the matter 
11  should be resolved in approximately four (4) months.  Pursuant to LR 26-1 and Fed. R. Civ. 
12  P.26(f), the Parties held the 26(f) Conference on November 14, 2025, and also discussed these
13  issues.  While the Plaintiff opposes both Motions and has filed its Oppositions (ECF Nos. 32
14  and 33), the Plaintiff does agree that the Court should resolve the critical preliminary
15  questions of jurisdiction and venue before any of the Parties spend the time and expense of
16  discovery in this case.                                                
17      The Discovery Plan and Scheduling Order was due on November 29, 2025.  In light of 
18  the pendency of the Motions, and L.R. 26-1, the Parties agreed that another 26(f) Conference 
19  should be held 21 days after a decision on the Motions to Dismiss and the deadline for the 
20  parties’ Discovery Plan and Scheduling Order should be extended until 14 days after the 
21  extended 26(f) Conference deadline, unless the Court orders otherwise.  The Parties filed a prior 
22  Stipulation regarding the Discovery Plan (ECF No. 43), which was denied without prejudice to 
23  allow the Parties to file this Stipulation through Minute Order (ECF No. 44). 
24      Although “[t]he Federal Rules of Civil Procedure do not provide for automatic or 
25  blanket stays of discovery when a potentially dispositive motion is pending,” “[c]ourts have 
26  broad discretionary power to control discovery,” Kor Media Grp., LLC v. Green, 294 F.R.D. 
27  579, 581 (D. Nev. 2013) (quoting Tradebay, LLC v. eBay, Inc., 278 F.R.D. 597, 601 (D. Nev. 
28  2011), and citing Little v. City of Seattle, 863 F.2d 681, 685 (9th Cir. 1988)).  The Court can, in 
1  its discretion, stay discovery for “good cause” under Rule 26. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(c); Clardy 
2  v. Gilmore, 773 F. App’x 958, 959 (9th Cir. 2019).  The Court should stay discovery if good
3  cause exists and doing so serves “the objectives of Rule 1 to ensure a ‘just, speedy, and
4  inexpensive determination of every action,’” see Kor Media Grp., 294 F.R.D. at 581 (quoting
5  Tradebay, 278 F.R.D. at 602–03).                                       
6      However, “[t]he Ninth Circuit has not provided a rule or test that district courts must 
7  apply to determine if good cause exists to stay discovery.”  See Salazar v. Honest Tea, Inc., No. 
8  2:13-CV- 02318-KJM-EFB, 2015 WL 6537813, at *1 (E.D. Cal. Oct. 28, 2015).  Thus, a party 
9  moving to stay discovery in this District must make a “strong showing why discovery should 
10  be denied” by satisfying three requirements:  (1) A pending motion is potentially dispositive of 
11  the action, 2) The pending dispositive motion “can be decided without additional discovery,” 
12  and (3) The Court, after taking “a ‘preliminary peek’ at the merits of the potentially dispositive 
13  motion,” is “convinced that the plaintiff will be unable to state a claim for relief.”  Kor Media 
14  Grp., 294 F.R.D. at 581 (citing Tradebay, 278 F.R.D. at 602–03).       
15      When the pending dispositive motion goes to personal jurisdiction, the Court “rel[ies] 
16  on a more lenient approach in the personal jurisdiction context.”  PlayUp, Inc. v. Mintas, 635 
17  F.Supp. 3d 1087, 1099 (D. Nev. 2022) (citing Kabo Tools Co. v. Porauto Indus. Co., No. 2:12-
18  CV-01859-LDG-NJK,  2013  WL  5947138,  at  *2  (D.  Nev.  Oct.  31,  2013));  see  also
19  CC.Mexicano.US, 2014 WL 12707483, at *1 (“Where the underlying motion to dismiss is
20  brought pursuant to Rule 12(b)(2) for lack of personal jurisdiction, a less rigorous standard is
21  applied … .”).  This more lenient standard also applies where a motion seeks dismissal for
22  improper  venue.    See,  e.g.,  Int’l  Markets  Live,  Inc.  v.  Halterman,  No.  2:18-CV-00187-
23  JADGWF, 2018 WL 11472563, at *1 (D. Nev. July 11, 2018).  In Kabo Tools, this Court noted
24  that  “a  pending  motion  challenging  personal  jurisdiction  strongly  favors  a  stay,  or  at  a
25  minimum, limitations on discovery until the question of jurisdiction is resolved.”  Kabo Tools,
26  2013 WL 5947138, at *2.  In other words, “courts are more inclined to stay discovery pending
27  resolution of a motion to dismiss challenging personal jurisdiction because it presents a ‘critical
28  preliminary question.’”  CC.Mexicano.US, 2014 WL 12707483, at *1.      
1      A stay of discovery is particularly appropriate in this case because judicial economy 
2  would be disserved by continuing litigation in this District particularly given the proceedings 
3  in India, and whether this District much less the United States is the proper forum.  The Court 
4  should, instead, stay discovery pending resolution of the pending Motions or at a minimum the 
5  proceedings in India.                                                  
6      This request is made in good faith and not for the purposes of delay. 
7  Dated this 5th day of December 2025.  Dated this 5th day of December 2025. 
8

2        Considering  the  stipulation  between  counsel,  and  with  good  cause  appearing,  the 
     Motion to Stay is GRANTED.  In the event that the resolution of the Motions to Dismiss do not 
4]|  result  in  the  dismissal  of these  two  defendants,  the  Parties  are  ordered  to  hold  another 
5||   scheduling conference required by Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f) 21 days after a decision on the pending 
6||  Defendants’ Motions to Dismiss (ECF Nos. 26 and 27) and the November 29, 2025 deadline 
7\|  for the parties’  Discovery Plan  and  Scheduling  Order is  extended until  14  days  after the 
     extended 26(f) Conference deadline. 
9        IT IS SO ORDERED.
